On the Sources and the Title

The present work, titled Uṣūl al-Ḥikmah, draws upon a number of classical sources within the broader literature of Islamic spiritual sciences. Its primary foundations are derived from Imām Aḥmad al-Būnī's Shams al-Maʿārif al-Kubrā and Manbaʿ Uṣūl al-Ḥikmah, two works that have long served as important references for the study of Divine Names, letter symbolism (ʿilm al-ḥurūf), invocations, correspondences, and spiritual practices associated with the Būnian tradition. Additional material has been informed by collections such as Majmūʿat al-Aḥzāb, which preserves devotional formulas and litanies transmitted through the spiritual heritage, as well as Uṣūl al-Basṭfī Sirr al-Awfāq wa al-Ḥawāṣṣ.

The title Uṣūl al-Ḥikmah was chosen deliberately. It does not imply that this work replaces, reproduces, or claims the authority of the original texts from which it draws. Rather, it reflects the intention of the compiler: to present a focused recension of selected foundational principles (uṣūl) underlying these sciences, arranged according to the themes and areas of emphasis most relevant to the intended reader. In this sense, the title refers not to a new claim of authorship, but to a gathering (compilation) of essential foundations of wisdom (ḥikmah) drawn from a wider inherited tradition.

Knowledge is of many kinds. There is knowledge that informs the

mind, knowledge that disciplines the limbs, and knowledge that purifies the heart. The scholars of every generation have distinguished between these forms of knowledge, for confusing their purposes can lead sincere seekers away from the path intended for them.

Among the inherited sciences of Islam is what later generations came to call ʿilm al-rūḥāniyyāt, the spiritual sciences concerned with the Divine Names, Qurʾanic invocations, healing, protection, and the subtle realities of creation. Like all sacred sciences, it has its etiquette (adab), its people, its chains of transmission (isnād), and its conditions. It was never intended to be pursued without discipline, guidance, and proper preparation.

This recension of the works of Imām Aḥmad al-Būnī is therefore a welcome contribution. Throughout the history of our spiritual traditions, knowledge was received through companionship, instruction, and authorization. Books preserve the memory of a tradition, but teachers preserve its understanding.

The seeker must therefore approach these sciences with humility. The opening of a manuscript is not the opening of a path. A text may describe methods and principles, but it cannot replace the guidance of those who have inherited the responsibility of teaching and correcting the seeker.

Our masters of taṣawwuf have always emphasized that extraordinary experiences are not the measure of spiritual attainment. Visions, unveilings, and unusual phenomena are secondary matters. The true fruit of the path is sincerity before Allah, purification of the heart, beautiful character, and service to creation. If the pursuit of rūḥāniyyāt assists these aims, it becomes a means of benefit; if it distracts from them, it becomes a veil.

The compiler, Amin Patel, has devoted years to the study and practice of rūḥāniyyāt under multiple teachers and, having received idhn in this discipline, has served his community as a practitioner of spiritual healing. In preparing this recension, he has rendered a valuable service by making these foundational materials freely available to serious students. Yet every reader should remember that no book can grant idhn, nor can written knowledge replace companionship with the people of Allah.

Imām al-Būnī occupies a distinguished place within the history of the Islamic spiritual sciences. He belonged to a civilisation in which scholarship, spirituality, and disciplined apprenticeship were inseparable. Traditional Sufi accounts also place him within the same broader Maghribī intellectual milieu as Shaykh Muḥyī al-Dīn Ibn ʿArabī, with both associated through their inheritance of ʿilm al-ḥurūf with the teaching of Shaykh ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz al-Mahdawī. Their works represent different expressions of a living tradition in which the outward and inward sciences were cultivated together under qualified masters.

Although this work draws from Shams al-Maʿārif and Manbaʿ Uṣūl al-Ḥikmah, it should be approached as a reference and companion to those works, not as a substitute for living instruction. The sciences of the spirit are preserved not only through books, but through sound intention, righteous companionship, and responsible transmission.

To those beginning this journey: rectify the apparent before seeking the hidden. Establish worship before seeking unveilings. Purify intention before seeking influence. If Allah has written a portion of these sciences for you, He will open the appropriate doors through the means He has chosen.
May Allah Most High grant us beneficial knowledge, protect us from knowledge that increases arrogance, illuminate our hearts with sincerity, and make every step a means of drawing nearer to Him.
The first edition of this work was completed in early 2021 as a highly

abridged synthesis of two of the most influential works of Shaykh Aḥmad al-Būnī: Shams al-Maʿārif and Manbaʿ Uṣūl al-Ḥikmah, and was released on the internet through various channels for free. The present edition, released in 2026, is substantially revised and expanded. While retaining the original aim of providing a practical reference to the foundational concepts of the Būnian tradition, it incorporates additional material, editorial refinements, and a deeper appreciation.

This work should not be mistaken for a curriculum of spiritual training. Like the classical texts from which it draws, it is intended as a reference rather than a manual capable of replacing a qualified teacher. The literature of rūḥāniyyāt has always functioned in conjunction with living transmission (talqīn), authorization (idhn), and disciplined practice and riyadah under appropriate guidance. Detached from that context, even the most celebrated texts reveal only part of the tradition they seek to preserve. Errors and misdirection in the manuscript, both deliberate and unintended are part and parcel of rūḥāniyyāt literature.

Looking back upon my own journey, I have come to appreciate that one does not simply choose the path of rūḥāniyyāt; rather, one finds oneself drawn toward it. Within qadar, there are paths that appear to open naturally for some while remaining closed to others despite sincere effort. The aspirant ultimately discovers that advancement in this discipline depends upon Divine permission before it depends upon personal determination.

For those who are also travellers upon the path of sulūk under the guidance of a kāmil shaykh, the extent to which the sciences of rūḥāniyyāt are cultivated is likewise governed by that spiritual training. Different ṭuruq have historically adopted different attitudes toward extraordinary spiritual phenomena such as kashf and other forms of unveiling. Some regard such experiences as secondary or even distracting when compared with the higher objective of attaining proximity to Allah through purification of the soul. Where one's teachers discourage such pursuits, wisdom lies in following their direction rather than attempting to force openings that do not belong to one's path.

My own rūḥāniyyāt teachers have been many, some living and others now departed. Throughout that journey, it is striking that the foundational texts of the thirteenth century were never employed as teaching manuals, not even once. Although works such as Shams al-Maʿārif and Manbaʿ Uṣūl al-Ḥikmah remain indispensable historical and intellectual landmarks, they function principally as repositories of principles, correspondences, and inherited methods. They were never intended to substitute for apprenticeship. Every student's development unfolds differently, often in a manner that is neither predictable nor linear.

Like taṣawwuf itself, rūḥāniyyāt is best understood as a living tradition rather than a closed historical system. One may reasonably view it as a specialized sub-branch within the broader framework of taṣawwuf, cultivated only by certain disciples according to aptitude, temperament, and the judgement of their teachers. Its purpose is not the pursuit of marvels (karāmāt) or extraordinary experiences for their own sake. The true aim of sulūk has always been maʿrifat Allāh, the experiential knowledge of Allah. Nevertheless, every community requires individuals capable of healing, spiritual counsel, and other specialized forms of service (khidma), and it is within this sphere that the disciplined study of rūḥāniyyāt has traditionally found its place, under a licensed mentor.

The methods preserved in al-Būnī's writings represent, in many respects, the technical vocabulary and operative conventions of their age. They remain invaluable for understanding the historical foundations of the discipline, yet no living tradition remains frozen in the century of its earliest texts. As generations of teachers inherit, refine, and transmit knowledge, methods evolve while remaining rooted in the same spiritual principles. Contemporary practitioners therefore inherit not only books but living chains of transmission (asānīd), practical disciplines (riyāḍāt), periods of retreat (khalwah), and authorizations received through their teachers.

Within many lineages, teachers speak of instruction received through the broader spiritual inheritance of their silsilah, whether through the fellowship of the righteous, the unseen company associated with their order and hadra, or souls from the alam al arwah, in some instances through the Ḥaḍrah al-Muḥammadiyyah, reserved for the elect adepts. Such matters belong to the experiential vocabulary of the tradition itself and cannot be authenticated or transmitted by books alone. They remain inseparable from the teacher-disciple relationship and from the ethical and spiritual disciplines that accompany it. The tradition is not “reconstructed” from books, ours, the rūḥāniyyāt tradion is a living one. One requires an inner and an outer contact. Let it be known that the path of a rūḥāniyyāt adept is not an easy one.

For this reason, no book can confer idhn. Authorization belongs to those qualified to grant it. Nor should this compilation be regarded as offering spiritual protection, practical competency, or permission to engage in practices that have traditionally required supervision. Those who pursue these sciences without appropriate guidance do so entirely upon their own responsibility, and at great personal risk, at times, irreversable.

Likewise, readers whose own ṭarīqah or teachers discourage the study of rūḥāniyyāt are encouraged to honour that guidance. Fidelity to one's shaykh and one's path takes precedence over curiosity. Every tradition possesses its own pedagogy and priorities, and spiritual progress is better served through obedience than through indiscriminate accumulation of knowledge.

This compilation has therefore been prepared simply as an act of khidmah: a freely offered reference for serious students (with a mentor) who may benefit from having in one compilation, a carefully selected recension of two foundational works. It is intended to accompany learning, not replace it; to illuminate principles, not confer mastery.

In the end, the sciences of rūḥāniyyāt, however subtle or profound, remain secondary to the greater journey. Where the path of rūḥāniyyāt reaches its horizon, the path of sulūk has, in many respects, only just begun. May we not get sidelined by “sidequests”.

May Allah grant every sincere seeker what is best for them, open the doors that are beneficial, close those that are harmful, and, if it is written in their decree, allow them to cross the threshold into these sciences with wisdom, humility, and sound guidance. Āmīn.

Prologue — The Conditions and Practice of This Science

[I 7] The Conditions and Practice of This Science The conditions of this science are founded upon the basic principles laid down by the scholars, and if these conditions are not observed, the workings performed will not come to pass. The secrets of Allah, the Exalted, lie in His letters, His names, and His noble verses, and He bestows these secrets upon His righteous servants. Indeed Allah, may He be glorified and exalted, declares this in the Noble Qur'an, Sūrat Ghafir (al-Mu'min), verse 60:
(Worship and call upon Me, that I may answer you)

There are certain conditions for working with this science of khawāṣṣ, and so long as these conditions are not fulfilled, a working that is carried out will never come to pass. The conditions of this blessed science are as follows:
1. Firm resolve: Never doubt a working that you are about to perform, for doubt spoils the working that is done. Our Prophet, Muḥammad (peace and blessings be upon him), said:
(Call upon Allah while certain that your
prayer will be answered.) In accordance with this noble hadith, one must begin the working with perfect faith and turn to Allah, Glorious is His Majesty, believing with the heart.

2. Patience: Without growing bored, tired, or weary, one must continue with full patience and concentration until the work one has begun ends in success. Allah, the Exalted, declares in the Noble Qur'an:

[I 8] (O you who believe! Be patient, and vie with one another in patience, and bind yourselves with your whole being to Allah, may He be glorified and exalted. And fear Allah, that you may attain salvation. Sūrat Āl 'Imrān, verse 200.)
For he who strives attains his goal, and every one who strives has his portion. Our Prophet, Muḥammad (peace and blessings be upon him), said:
He who is patient attains victory.
3. Keeping the secret: You must tell no one, and let no one sense, what you are about to do, what you are reciting, or what work you are engaged in. Muḥammad (peace and blessings be upon him) said:

(Seek help in the fulfillment of your needs by keeping your secret.) Perform the working in a secluded place where no one can see you. Never say to anyone, "I did such and such," or "I do such and such!" The saying of Hazrat Omer (may Allah be pleased with him), "He who keeps his secret is safe from harm," is well known.
4. Being God-fearing: Rising on the spiritual path and attaining success come through piety and God-consciousness (takva), for Allah declares in Sūrat Tā-Hā, verse 132:
(A good end is attained through piety.)

This means not eating what is forbidden, eating and drinking only what is lawful, avoiding and refraining from backbiting, not lying, giving importance to truthfulness and sincere counsel, not looking upon others with an evil eye, not tormenting people while bearing torment oneself, and looking upon people with compassion and mercy.

5. Not being hasty: Perform the working you intend to do without haste, with tranquility of heart, free from every thought in your mind (family, wealth, [I 9] joy, fear, grief, and the like), gathering your strength, your resolve (himma), your will, and your desire upon a single point, so that your aim may be fulfilled. Do the work you undertake with love and willingness. No good comes of work done carelessly, as a mere formality.

6. Being clean: You must be in a constant state of ritual purity, and pay great attention to the cleanliness of your body, your clothing, and the place where you are and above all, the cleanliness of your heart.
7. Being licensed: It is essential that the person carrying out this work hold an icazet (a master's authorization). A person without icazet is like a fatherless child.

8. Identifying: When you wish to perform a working of love, attraction, separation, affliction, spirit-sending, summoning, causing illness, healing the sick, or the like upon someone, you identify — that is, come to know — that person's complexion, appearance, height, and whether they are old or young. If you do not know these things, you write using the name of the person's mother instead. If you do not know the mother's name either, you take it to be Havva (Eve) and write accordingly. Identification is more effective than merely giving a name, and more effective still is to use identification and names together.

9. Practicing ascetic discipline (riyada): One must not eat the meat of animals or animal products such as milk, honey, and eggs, nor onions, garlic, or foods of similarly foul odor, and the stomach must be neither empty nor stuffed to excess.
10. Having spiritual resolve (himma): Do not make a tool of exalted things for base purposes! For Allah, the Exalted, declares in Sūrat al-Baqara, verse 41:
(Do not sell My verses for a paltry price.) Do not use the verses of Allah, the Exalted, for evil deeds or evil intentions!

11. Knowing the time of the working: Determine carefully the day and hour of the working to be performed, in accordance with the properties of the planets. Furthermore, the day of the working must not be an inauspicious day. In every lunar month, the 3rd, 5th, 13th, 16th, 21st, 24th, and 25th days are inauspicious days. Do not perform beneficial workings on these menkut days! Beneficial workings should be done on the days when the light of the moon is increasing, while harmful workings should be done on the days when the moon is waning [I 10] (the last three nights of every lunar month).
12. Facing the qibla: When performing a working, write while facing the qibla, the direction of prayer toward Mecca. Arrange the writing according to the original and place each element correctly.

If the writing is a name or a noble verse, a word or letter that comes later must not be moved earlier, nor may a word or letter that comes earlier be moved later. Moreover, the handwriting must be very fine. If a wafq is being written, the numbers or letters must be placed according to the order of the wafq's cells, the numbers or letters must be written beautifully, and the cells of the wafq must be drawn equal to one another.

13. Invoking blessings upon the Prophet: Before and after every working, invoke the noble salawat upon Muḥammad (peace and blessings be upon him). Our Prophet, Muḥammad Mustafa (peace and blessings be upon him), said on this matter:
(A supplication made between two salawat is never turned away.)
The following blessed salawat is highly meritorious:

(O Allah, send blessings upon our master and liege-lord Muḥammad, the Prophet, and upon his family and Companions, and grant them peace — blessings as numerous as Your creation, as pleasing to You, as heavy as Your Throne, and as abundant as the ink of Your words.)

14. Istikhara: If you perform the istikhara prayer before every working, you will act with insight in the work you undertake. The istikhara is performed as follows: you pray two rak'ahs. In the first rak'ah you recite al-Fātiḥa together with Sūrat al-Kafirun, and in the second rak'ah al-Fātiḥa together with Sūrat al-Ikhlāṣ; after giving the salam, you recite the following istikhara supplication three, five, or seven times. The istikhara supplication to be recited is this:
I 11] (... ḥājati) — In the phrase written within]) .the parentheses, you insert whatever your need actually is

(O God, I seek Your guidance through Your knowledge, and I seek ability through Your power, and I ask of You from Your immense bounty, that You make plain to me the outcome of this matter — of such-and-such a thing, and here he mentions his need. If it is good for me, then open my breast to it and grant me success in accomplishing it; and if it is bad, then turn it away from me and turn me away from it, for You have power over all things.)
If you find ease and peace in your heart, you carry out the working (amal) believing that you will succeed in it and reach your goal.

But if your spirit feels constricted, you abandon it. Persisting anyway will only work to your harm. The istihare (the prayer for divine guidance) must be performed fully awake and with the heart believing in the power of God Most High, for He alone knows the truth of things and how they will end.

15. Not employing the spirits (ruhaniyyun) in base tasks: If you try to employ the spirits for base and unworthy works, you will have insulted and demeaned them. Because the spirits act according to the Sacred Law (sheriat), they will not carry out any working that is doubtful. Never attempt to employ them in matters contrary to the Sacred Law! Also, do not go asking the spirits about every need you have.

Memorizing the azaim (conjuration formulas): The azaim you will recite to the spirits (rūḥāniyya) must also be memorized thoroughly, and you must not stammer at all while reciting them. It is not enough to read the ʿazīma from a book or from a tablet (lawḥ), for then the heart becomes occupied with the writing and the necessary reverent absorption (hushu') is lost. This in turn removes concentrated attention (tewejjuh), which is the most essential of the pillars (erkan) of the working.

17. How the working is carried out: If, in a working you undertake, you need to write upon a tablet (lawḥ), you inscribe the writing onto the tablet with an iron stylus (mil). If it is on paper or leather, you write with a reed pen (kamish). When you cut the tip of the reed pen, you say three times, [I 12] and having said it, you recite the following noble verse, the third verse of Surah at-Talaq:

.And whoever puts his trust in God — He is sufficient for him) Indeed, God accomplishes His purpose; God has set a measure for all things.) You recite this. After cutting the tip of the reed pen, you take the pen in your hand and say:
(I have cut my pen for the sake of such-and-such a working.)
In place of "such-and-such," you say whatever your purpose actually is. If you recite the noble verse first, the working becomes more effective and more potent.

If the working you are performing is for love or attraction (mahabba), and the planetary natures of the maṭlūb (the object of the working) and the talib (the seeker, the one on whose behalf the working is done) are friendly to one another, you write both of their names. If their planets are enemies to one another, you write only the name of the maṭlūb, and do not write the name of the talib.

After these conditions, let us explain the calculation of abjad (the numerical alphabet), the elements (ʿanāṣir) of the twenty-eight letters, the luminous (nurani) and dark (zulmani) letters, the natures of the elements, their friendship and enmity with one another, the properties of the planets, their friendship and enmity, their letters, their incenses (bakhūr), and also their fortune (said)

and misfortune (nahis) and their exaltation (sheref). After that, let us clearly explain the properties of the zodiacal signs (burjh), their friendship and enmity, the mansions of the moon, in which sign the moon is found, and in which sign the sun is found — so that those who seek this science may understand it easily.

Abjad table of letter-number values — eight rows read right to left, alternating a row of Arabic letters with a row giving each letter's numerical value, running from the units through the tens, hundreds and thousands. no labels. [I 13]
Concerning abjad, Hazrat Ali (may God be pleased with him) has said:
(Learn the rules of abjad, its numerical values, and the methods of its use, for through them many wondrous mysteries come to light.)
In the Abjad al-Kabir — the most widely used, and the original, principal abjad — the numbers run one by one from one (1) to ten (10). This is the Abjad al-Kabir (Great Abjad).

Abjad table with reduced letter values — rows alternate Arabic letters with their assigned numbers; the only word is "Sakit" ("fallen away, void"), marking letters to which no value is assigned. [I 14]

This abjad is called Abjad Saghir (Lesser Abjad). This lesser abjad is derived from the greater abjad. If twelve (12) is subtracted, twelve at a time, from the numerical value of each letter in the Abjad al-Kabir, the number that remains is that letter's equivalent.

For example: the letter Lam has the value thirty in the Abjad Kabir. If we subtract twelve, twelve at a time, from this number, six remains. The equivalent of the letter Lam in the Abjad Saghir is six (6). The letter Ra has the value two hundred (200) in the Abjad Kabir. If we subtract twelve (12), twelve at a time, from this number, eight (8) remains. The equivalent of the letter Ra in the Abjad Saghir (Lesser Abjad) is eight (8).
This is the Abjad Saghir (Lesser Abjad):

In the Abjad Saghir, four letters are sakit (dropped, literally "fallen"). These four letters are Sin, Shīn, Khāʾ, and Ẓāʾ. If we subtract twelve, twelve at a time, from these letters' values in the Abjad Kabir, zero remains. For this reason these four letters are sakit.
Abjad table of expanded letter values — rows alternate Arabic letters with the numerical value of each letter's fully spelled-out name (alif written out = 111, and so on). no labels. [I 15]
[I 15] THE GREAT JUMMAL ABJAD (Abjad jummal kabīr)

The Great Jummal Abjad is calculated according to the numeric values of the letters' own names. For example: the letter Jīm is written and named "Jīm," which is made up of three letters. The sum of the numeric values of these three letters is (3 + 10 + 40 = 53). The letter Qāf is written and named "Qāf," which is likewise made up of three letters. The sum of the numeric values of these three letters is: Qāf 100, Alif 1, and the letter Fe 80, totaling 181.
The Great Abjad value of the letter Qāf is 181.
This is the Abjad jummal kabīr (Great Jummal Abjad):
In the name of Allah, the All-Merciful, the Compassionate, and may God bless our master Muḥammad and his family and his Companions, and grant them peace.

A testimony of pre-eternity (azal)! From the light of this testimony the elect have scooped up knowledge — so understand that. And the everlasting ordering lies in the two testimonies conjoined with [the testimony of] the noble angels, those possessed of knowledge; this, then, is the testimony of everlastingness (abad). Whoever grasps the secret of these two testimonies beholds the two dominions; then I have entrusted to him the secret of connection with the unveilings (kashfiyyāt), and every configuration that conveys him to all the matters of wisdom.
And I ask of God, the Living, the Self-Subsisting (al-Ḥayy al-Qayyūm), that He make it an alms accepted before my intimate discourse [with

Him]; that He grant me the companionship of the spirit of His gladdening in my going to and fro and in my resting place; that He make the way plain to me and to you, and favour us and you with the lights of realization (taḥqīq). Truly this flash of Mercy (al-barqa al-raḥamūtiyya) and these shining, luminous suns are the ways of the gnostics, the highway of the veracious, and the very heart of those who set their course for the holy Presence of the Lord of the Worlds — God of the first and of the last, Lord of lords, who rends open the causes and lifts the veil, the Originator without any model, transcendent above genera and forms, the Everlasting who has never ceased and shall never cease to be qualified by the descriptions of perfection, perpetual in existence in pre-eternity, who raises up the celestial realms by His determining and His wisdom and spreads out the terrestrial realms by His power and His will. There is no god but He, the Great, the Most High (al-Kabīr al-Mutaʿāl), veiled behind the veils of the lights, hidden from all secrets, concealed from the pavilions of sight. He was inward with respect to His Essence in His pre-eternity, and became manifest through His attributes in His everlastingness; He made Himself openly known through His names in His sempiternity, and disclosed Himself through His acts in His duration. He is the First in pre-eternity, the Last in everlastingness, and the Manifest in sempiternity. He is exalted beyond substances and accidents, beyond parts and portions, and beyond acting for any purpose. The directions and the regions do not contain Him; the succession of the motions of the cycles does not wear Him away; the passing of night and day does not annihilate Him — glorified and exalted is He. Everything with Him is by measure; He is the Knower of the unseen and the witnessed, the Great, the Most High.

And I bear witness that there is no god but God alone, who has no partner a testimony that accompanies the spirits with steadfastness in the intermediate states (barzakhiyyāt). He has known the full reckoning of His creation, the living and the dead; He has apportioned the provisions and the sustenance; He knows what has passed and what is to come, and He brings the dead to life after they have become crumbled remains. And I bear witness that our master Muḥammad is His servant and His Messenger, the sun of the religious community, the deliverer of [God's] servants from associationism (shirk) and from abasement, who set the sphere of the divine oneness (tawḥīd) turning by his summons. The crescent moons of religion took their light from the suns of his wisdom; the stars of error sank away at the sight of him; and the morning of those who affirm God's oneness broke bright through his felicity. May God bless him and his family and his Companions with the most excellent of enduring blessings, and may God, exalted is He, be well pleased with the Companions, the realizers, the veracious — may God be pleased with them all — with a blessing that conveys them to the highest ranks and the loftiest degrees. To proceed: the Truth has its guiding marks, and Reality has its order, and the spirits have an earnest concern for the divine gnoses. Excellence is a thing sought after, and the power to acquire it is a thing bestowed; felicity is conjoined with the suns of perfection; and everlasting life is pledged upon (marhūna bi-) the employment of the observances of the sacred Law. The highest of the degrees in ʿIlliyyūn are the degrees of the learned and of those who act; and the highest of them in degree and station is that of the guides, the realizers. There is no station in the religion of God for a scholar who gives no benefit, just as there is no existence of life for the reality of a soul that receives no benefit. And the furthest of people from felicity is he who makes light of the ordinances of the religious community and neglects the conditions [laid down by] the realizers among the people of the qibla.

Now, when I saw that each of the masters — those whose word has stood high, whose wisdom has spread abroad through the horizons, and whose blessing has extended over all created beings — had composed works upon the operative deployment (taṣrīf) of the names, upon the secrets of the letters, the litanies of remembrance, and the invocations; and when one whose affection was bound to me besought me to make plain to him the secret of what they had composed and the treasure of what they had laid up: then I answered him — while acknowledging my incapacity to comprehend the apprehensions of the forebears who have passed away and of the realizing, guiding imāms — and I hoped from God, through the offering of confession and of [acknowledged] wrongdoing, that He would supply me from the spirits of their spirits with a subtlety of succour, so that the utterance might accord with realization and be joined to the tongue of affirmation.

So I say — and in God is help sought: Know that the aim of the chapters of this book is that thereby there may be known the nobility of the names of God, exalted is He, and what God, exalted is He, has deposited in their sea of the various kinds of gems of wisdom and divine subtleties, and how the operative use of the names of the invocations is made, together with what follows upon them of the letters of the suras and the verses. I have set this book out in chapters, so that each chapter may point to what it encompasses and has enumerated of the subtle sciences by which one attains connection to the Lordly Presence without toil and without incurring hardship, and to what among them leads on to the desirable things of this world and to what is desired therein. And I have named this blessed and choice book — without peer, exalted in learning "The Sun of Gnosis and the Subtleties of Benefactions" because of what it holds within it of the subtleties of the operative deployments and the benefactions of the efficacious influences. It is therefore forbidden to anyone into whose hand this book of mine falls to show it to one who is not fit for it, or to divulge it to one who does not deserve it; for whenever he does that, God, exalted is He, will deprive him of its benefits, and its advantages and its blessing will be withheld from him. Beware of touching it while you are not in a state of purity. Do not read it save as one engaged in remembrance [of God], and do not put it to operative use save in that wherein God's good pleasure lies. Beware of anything other than obedience, lest you be stripped of its secret and denied its blessing; for it is the book of the friends of God (awliyāʾ), the righteous, the obedient, the aspirants, those who act, and those who yearn. So be chary of it, and relinquish nothing of it, little or much. Let your certainty be true and your faith in its realities firm: ((Deeds are only by intentions, and every man shall have only what he intended.)) And when an intention arises in you for one of the operations, then have faith in it and hold it true, in accordance with his saying — upon him be blessing and peace — ((Let none of you supplicate except while he is certain of being answered.)); and judge your operation to be sound, in accordance with his saying — upon him be blessing and peace — ((When one of you asks his Lord, let him be resolute in the asking, for there is none who can compel Him.)); and be certain of the answer, and judge your operation to be sound, in accordance with his saying — God bless him and grant him peace — ((One of you will be answered so long as he does not grow hasty and say: I have supplicated and I have not been answered.)) Beware of reckoning the answer slow in coming; rather, remain ever waiting and watching for its appearance.

This upright canon and straight path comprises forty chapters, each set out in detail, every chapter comprising meanings, indications, and symbols both hidden and manifest. So ponder them with your intellect.

I say and from God is help sought, and upon Him is reliance placed: the aims of those who seek [this knowledge] fall into two divisions, the worldly and the otherworldly, and each of the two is further divided into sections according to the purposes intended. People had discoursed upon the matching (muʿāraḍa) of awfāq, upon the observation of the planets, upon the ascetic disciplines (riyāḍāt), and upon the operations of talismans, before this book was composed and before there was any discussion of it. This is a broad science, one that many people have desired, worked with, and persevered in — especially any who have found some effect in it. So I wished to set over against that a description that runs in the manner of an occult property (khāṣṣa), within the direction taken by the practitioners of the science just mentioned, of

which the ancient sages spoke and with which statement many people have agreed. For those [other practices], if they produce an effect in this world, do harm in the next; whereas this which we set forth is of benefit both in this world and in the next. And God is the granter of success in what is right.
Chapter 1 (al-bāb al-awwal): On the letters of the alphabet (ḥurūf al- muʿjam) and the secrets and concealments (iḍmārāt) they contain

Faṣl. In it I speak first of the letters of the alphabet, since they are the roots of speech and its foundation, and by them its edifice is raised up. Know that numbers have secrets, just as letters have effects, and that the upper world supplies the lower world. For the world of the Throne supplies the world of the Footstool; the world of the Footstool supplies the sphere of Saturn; the sphere of Saturn supplies the sphere of Jupiter; the sphere of Jupiter supplies the sphere of Mars; the sphere of Mars supplies the sphere of the Sun; the sphere of the Sun supplies the sphere of Venus; the sphere of Venus supplies the sphere of Mercury; the sphere of Mercury supplies the sphere of the Moon; the sphere of the Moon supplies the sphere of heat; the sphere of heat supplies the sphere of air; the sphere of air supplies the sphere of water; and the sphere of water supplies the sphere of earth. To Saturn, among the celestial [letters], belongs the letter (jīm), and the numbers that fall to it are three in sum; but in detail, fifty-three, thus: the mīm as forty, the yāʾ as ten, and the jīm as three — and it is likewise [written] with three letters. To it, among the terrestrial [letters], belongs the letter (ṣād), which in number is ninety; and to it belongs the threefold square (al-muthallath). To the sphere of Jupiter belongs the letter (dāl), which is four in number, and to it belongs the fourfold square (al-murabbaʿ), which is four multiplied by four. The operative deployment of the sphere of Mars, among the celestial [letters], is five in sum; it is the letter (hāʾ), and of the awfāq it has the fivefold (al-mukhammas). To the sphere of the Sun belongs six; it is the letter (wāw), and of the awfāq it has the sixfold (al-musaddas). As for the operative deployment of the sphere of Venus, [it is] seven; it is the letter (zāy), and of the awfāq it has the sevenfold (al-musabbaʿ). As for the operative deployment of the sphere of Mercury, it has of number eight; it is the letter (ḥāʾ), and of the awfāq it has the eightfold (al-muthamman). As for the operative deployment of the sphere of the Moon, it has /fol. 4r./ of number nine; it is the letter (ṭāʾ), and of the awfāq it has the ninefold (al-mutassaʿ). And Saturn has the threefold square that is renowned among the learned. Understand, and you will be rightly guided.

Faṣl, on the relation of the human essence. The Throne has the letter (alif); the Footstool has the letter (bāʾ); Saturn has the letter (jīm); and so likewise on down to the Moon, according to what has been set out before it. Understand.

Faṣl. The letters are of [several] kinds. Some of them are begun from the right — these are the letters of the Arabs; and some of them are begun from the left — these are the Byzantine, the Greek, and the Coptic. Every script written toward the right is joined, and every script written toward the left is disjoined and not connected. Understand.

Faṣl. The letters are twenty-eight, apart from lām-alif, with which they come to a full twenty-nine; and that is the number of the lunar mansions. And since fourteen of the mansions appear above the earth, so likewise among these letters there are those that are assimilated to the lām of the definite article — fourteen letters, namely these:
; and there are those that appear distinctly with it, likewise fourteen letters, namely these: .

Faṣl. The first of the letters is the alif, and those letters that come after it — such as the ṭāʾs, the taʿrīfāt, and the rāʾs — are from the flanks of the alif. When one looks upon the letters, he finds that they leave an impress upon the soul, so that they come to exist in the soul before they exist in [outward] shape. The alif among the letters is the one among the numbers, and numbers possess a spiritual and subtle power. Numbers are among the secrets of words, just as letters are among the secrets of acts. Numbers have, in the human world, secrets and benefits which the

Maker — exalted be His power — has set in order, just as He set in order within the letters the secrets of benefit, such as invocation and incantations (ruqā) and other things whose effect has appeared in the sensible world through the various kinds of names. And know that no time confines the letters; rather they act by [their] occult property for whoever wishes [to employ them], whereas the numbers act by the natures, and so they are bound up with the celestial elections (ikhtiyārāt).

The letter (dāl) has of numbers four. So whoever sets up a figure of four multiplied by four and places within it a numerical proportion — and that on the day of Monday, the day of the Prophet's birth, God bless him and grant him peace, the day of his mission, and the day of his death — and let that be while the Moon is in its exaltation at three degrees of Taurus, free of the malefics, and while the hour is the Moon's: you write it after the purity of ablution and a prayer of two rakʿas with the Throne Verse and And say: He is God, One (Q 112:1) one hundred times, upon clean parchment. Whoever carries this written wafq with him, God — exalted is He — will make easy for him memorization, understanding, and wisdom, and his worth will be magnified in the eyes of the upper world and the lower world entire. And if a prisoner hangs it upon himself, he goes forth from his prison forthwith /fol. 4v./. And if this parchment is carried upon a banner, the enemies among the unbelievers and the rebellious are routed by it. And whoever carries it with him and disputes while holding it overcomes his adversary — because this letter, which is the dāl, has as the numbers that fall to it four, and its figure is four multiplied by four. And dirya(?) — Jupiter has special claim to it, and it is a benefic planet. The dāl is, in sum, a cold letter; and by it God completed the four natures — fire, air, water, and earth — which are yellow bile, blood, phlegm, and black bile. These, then, are four for four; and so it possesses the power of the natures and their equilibrium. This noble letter appears in His name al-Dāʾim (the Everlasting) in particular, and in His name al-Wadūd (the Loving) in general, since affection (wudd) is shared while everlastingness stands alone. For that reason the wāw comes before [the dāl] in al-Wadūd, whereas in al-Dāʾim nothing comes before the dāl.

And for that reason it occurs in the two noble and mighty names, Aḥmad and Muḥammad — God bless him and grant him peace — and that at the end of the two noble and generous names; because it points to everlastingness and to the last of the ultimate end: there is no god but He. So it is, after the dāl, for everlastingness. It comes first in His name al-Dāʾim only because to Him belongs perpetuity, first and last; and so He gave His servants a share in the perpetuity of subsistence in the hereafter, after annihilation. This letter is one of the letters of the Throne, because the Throne's existence does not alter, since it is the first of the world of originations and the first of the world of everlasting duration. To it are the ascents of the spirits; in it are the ranks of the intellects; and in it are the lights of Mercy. Most of the gnostics of God — exalted is He — have had this unveiled to them, according to the portion apportioned to them. Among them is Ḥāritha — may God, exalted is He, be pleased with him — when the Messenger of God, God bless him and grant him peace, questioned him and said to him: ((How have you risen this morning, O Ḥāritha? Ḥāritha said: O Messenger of God, I have risen a true believer. The Messenger of God, God bless him and grant him peace, said to him: Every truth has a reality; what is the reality of your faith? He said: I have risen having turned my soul away from this world, so that its stone and its gold are alike in my sight, and its living and its dead, and its rich and its poor; and it is as though I were looking upon the Throne of the All-Merciful brought forth into view, and upon the people being driven to the Reckoning — to the Garden and to the Fire. The Messenger of God, God bless him and grant him peace, said to him: You have known; now hold fast.)) And the Prophet — God bless him and grant him peace — said concerning the spirits: ((When they pass the night in the purity of ablution, they spend the night prostrate beneath the Throne.))

The letter dāl has among its secrets perpetuity and subsistence; and al-Dāʾim is a name among the names of God, exalted is He, [the name of] pre-eternity and post-eternity, and none but God, exalted is He, is named by it. As for al-Wadūd, affection is shared, as has preceded — and that is because affection (wudd) is the outward of love (ḥubb), and love is the inward of affection; so the first of affection is love (maḥabba). Affection divides into two divisions, an outward and an inward: its outward is affection and its inward is love. The dwelling place of affection is the heart, and it is the most disclosive of the worlds of the heart. Passionate love (ʿishq) is a subtlety between love and affection; its dwelling place is the pericardium (shaghaf). And love is the inward of passionate love, and its dwelling place is /fol. 5r./ the inmost heart (fuʾād) — for the heart has three cavities. The first of them is in its upper part, in that which is dense of it; it is a light that blazes up, and it is the locus of islām, and the meanings of the letters there are obscure. It is also the seat of the rational faculty in man and of the faculty that governs the meanings of the volition arising from the soul. The second is in the middle of the heart; it is the seat of reflection and recollection, and it is a shining light, and it is the seat of the indwelling peace (sakīna), and it is the seat of imagination with respect to what the spirit casts into it. The third is at its far end; it is the thinnest and subtlest of them, and it is denoted by the term fuʾād. It is the seat of faith, of the intellect, of light, of operative disposal, and of the secrets; [it is] the balance of the intellect and the subtleties of the wisdoms. It is the seat of love, and the seat of natural life deriving from the subtle heat.

This fuʾād has a luminous eye by which it apprehends the realities of the things of the Dominion (malakūt) and the secrets of the celestial things of the Omnipotence (jabarūt), and the balances of the realities. It is the seat of the lights of divine bestowal and of the secrets of the celestial things; and that is the inner sight (baṣīra) by which one sees. He said: For truly it is not the eyes that go blind, but rather it is the hearts within the breasts that go blind (Q 22:46). And the middle cavity — it is the seat of passionate love, and it is a luminous eye by which seeking is apprehended, and from it there arises earnestness in seeking and yearning for the thing sought; and it is the quickest to attach itself to persons.

— on account of its subtlety. By it the world of sovereign rule (ʿālam al-mulk) and all that it contains of the handiwork of God — exalted is He — is unveiled, and by it there comes about the finding of beauty in things beautiful. Then, to the first cavity there belongs a luminous eye by which it looks upon the secrets of sensible things, the phases of composite things, the realities of the letters and their secrets, and the immensity of what God — exalted is He — has deposited in them of the secrets of the names and the realities of the gnoses they impart. By it came its affection (wudd) for the servants of God, and its magnifying of God — exalted is He — on account of its knowledge, by reason of what God — exalted is He — has graciously bestowed upon it in its unveiling of the secrets of sensible things. These are the inner sights (baṣāʾir) of the hearts, all of them; save that men are disparate in the divergence of their states. We have already set forth in Mawāqīt al-baṣāʾir wa-laṭāʾif al-sarāʾir ("The Appointed Times of the Inner Sights and the Subtleties of the Innermost Secrets") that the spirits of revelation in the Book of God — exalted is He — are three: the Trustworthy Spirit (al-rūḥal-amīn), the Holy Spirit (rūḥal-qudus), and the Spirit of the Command (rūḥal-amr). The revelation from the Trustworthy Spirit descended upon the first cavity, because it is the isthmus (barzakh) that lies between speech and the tongue; and so it is the first of the degrees of revelation in the sending-down, each receiving according to what God has apportioned to him of God's inspiration upon the hearts. After it comes the Holy Spirit, and it pours forth the lights of what is set down in the Preserved Tablet upon the second degree of the heart, so that faith and intellective insight are made firm, and the kinds of wisdom, the kinds of Lordly supplies, and the subtleties of faith appear. Then the third degree, which is the locus of the most holy light; and it is likewise the locus of hearing, and it is the locus of the intellect. God — exalted is He — said to His prophet Muḥammad, God bless him and grant him peace, in His Mighty Book: For you cannot make the dead hear, nor can you make the deaf hear the call (Q 30:52). By that He did not intend the death of sense-perception; He intended by it only the death of unbelief and disobedience. /fol. 5v./ Nor did He intend by "the deaf" a deafness of the ears, for the faculty of hearing is present; He intended by it only this hearing which is in the world of the inmost heart (fuʾād), and that is the locus of the intellect and the locus of the descent of the Spirit of the Command, which points to empowerment (tamkīn) and to the reality of union (jamʿ); and none was singled out for this sending-down save Muḥammad, God bless him and grant him peace. We have expounded the valleys of the hearts, their treasuries, their lights, and their inner sights in our book known as Mawāqif al-ghāyāt fī asrār al-riyāḍāt ("The Stations of the Ultimate Ends, on the Secrets of the Spiritual Disciplines"); ponder it there and you will find it soundly set out, if God — exalted is He — wills. God — exalted is He — said: Those who believe and do righteous deeds — the All-Merciful will appoint for them affection (Q 19:96): that is, He brings into being in their hearts an affection by which they show affection to Him. This is because they instil affection into their hearts by the varieties of the litanies of remembrance (adhkār) and the modes of the acts of drawing near, so that they leave nothing of the works of the heart which they do not put to operative use; and they instil affection into their souls only by severing habits and familiar attachments, until there accrues to them an affection from God — exalted is He — so that their speech turns into the utterance of wisdom and their movements into an ascent of degrees. And he instils affection into his spirit by the realities of faith, the secrets of the revealed Law, and the lights of religion, until the traces of affection appear upon the spirit; then he beholds the Return by unveiling, and what God — exalted is He — has prepared therein of the kinds of bliss for His friends and of chastisement for His enemies, so that its flame increases in the seeking of the return to God, glorified and exalted, and in the longing for the meeting with God — exalted is He. And he instils affection into his intellect by reflecting upon the things God — exalted is He — has fashioned, and upon what God, blessed and exalted, has deposited in them of the secrets of His signs; and he instils affection into it by abandoning all entanglements and familiar attachments; and he instils affection into it by complying with His command, since it rests upon the root of purity, and commands only good and knows only good. And when the heart turns toward affection, it comes to gaze upon the secrets of the wonders of the Dominion (malakūt), upon the modes of the revelatory and inspirational addresses, and upon the celestial realities. We have gone on at length.

Let us now return to what we were about, concerning the letter dāl and its benefits. It is this: whoever writes the letter dāl thirty-five times — that being the number which falls to it when it is spelled out in detail, for when you write dāl in full the lām is thirty, the dāl is four, and the alif is one, so that the total is thirty-five — together with its square figure, upon a white silk cloth, and encircles it with the letter dāl thirty-five times, the Moon being in the house of Cancer and safeguarded from Jupiter, and sets it inside the bezel of a ring at that time, and wears it in a state of ritual purity, of fasting, and of inward clarity: God — exalted is He — will perpetuate for him the favour in which he stands, and will establish him in every outward undertaking, and God will make his provision ample. And whoever multiplies the remembrance of His name al-Dāʾim (the Everlasting) shall have that. We have mentioned this and expounded it in sum, under the name al-Dāʾim and the dāl of al-ḥamd (praise), in our book ʿIlm al-hudā wa-asrār al-ihtidāʾ ("The Science of Right Guidance and the Secrets of Being Guided"), under His name al-Raḥmān; so I need not repeat it.

And whoever draws it in this form, as its explanation will follow, and carries it with him, will attain all his aims and what he seeks from kings and rulers; women will love him and he will obtain from them an abundant share; and no woman will look upon him but she will love him, by the leave of God — exalted is He. And this is its form: /fol. 6r./
[Figure.1 — talismanic figure, as in the source; not reproduced in the text stream, ]

Some of them have mentioned that whoever writes "Muḥammad is the Messenger of God, Aḥmad is the Messenger of God" thirty-five times after the Friday prayer and carries it with him, God — exalted is He —

will grant him strength for obedience and aid unto blessing, and will suffice him against the promptings of the satans. And if he keeps up his gazing upon that slip (biṭāqa) while calling to mind the name of the Prophet — God bless him and grant him peace — Muḥammad, and his name Aḥmad, and how these two noble names, magnified, venerated, and blessed, were completed by this noble letter, namely the dāl, and if he persists in gazing upon them both every day at sunrise while invoking blessings upon the Prophet — God bless him and grant him peace — our master Muḥammad, God will make easy for him on that day of his the means of felicity. That is in proportion to [his] receptivity, to the resolve of intention, and to inward clarity; and this is a very subtle secret. And whoever writes the numerical square figure and carries it, God — exalted is He — will keep him safe from harmful enemies, from whichever of the worlds they may be. And whoever writes it, washes it off, and gives it to drink to one afflicted with an unremitting fever, that will benefit him; likewise it alleviates the pain of the venom for one stung by scorpions or bitten by serpents, and other such matters as befit this chapter. And this is the form of the square that has been mentioned:

As for its literal square figure, its occult property is that it takes away forgetfulness and sharpens the understanding and the intellect, for whoever persists in drinking it in rainwater and bees' honey. It also benefits one who suffers in his chest. And if it is engraved — with the Moon in Scorpio and Mars looking upon it with a look of enmity — upon a plate of copper which you heat in the fire, it is efficacious for the scorpion's sting, if its water is given to drink after the ring has been dipped in it.

Now since this square figure is the sum of the four alifs, which are the secret of the intellect, the secret of the spirit, the secret of the soul, and the secret of the heart — for the alif in number is one, and when you multiply the four by itself it spreads out to sixteen — that is the limit of the number taken in detail, because the Throne, the Footstool, the seven heavens and the seven earths: the total is sixteen. And this number is the limit of this square figure, which is sixteen cells. So within this sixteen there is the evenness (shafʿiyya) of fourteen, namely the seven heavens and the seven earths. And within it there is the evenness of twelve, namely the twelve zodiacal signs. And within it there is the evenness of eight, which is the evenness of the Bearers of the Throne. And within it there is the evenness of six, which is the evenness of the bodily bounds, namely: above, below, behind, in front, right, and left. And within it there is the evenness of four, which is the evenness of the prophets, the truthful ones, the martyrs, and the righteous. And within it there is the evenness of two, namely the testimony that there is no god but God and that Muḥammad is the Messenger of God. These, then, are seven evens. And within it there is, of the odd, the odd number (watr) fifteen, which is the Footstool, the seven heavens and the seven earths. And within it there is the odd number thirteen, which is the oddness of the Pen, the Tablet, the Trumpet, the Holy Spirit, the Footstool, and the seven heavens. And within it there is the oddness of eleven, which is what is in the world of man: the five senses — namely hearing, sight, smell, taste, and touch — and the six directions: above, below, right, left, behind, and in front. And within it there is the odd number nine, which is the essence of man and his eight natures, namely heat and dryness and cold and moisture, and heat and moisture and cold and dryness, and heat and dryness and cold and moisture; for yellow bile is hot and dry, and air is hot and moist — that being the nature of blood — and phlegm's nature is cold and moist, and black bile is cold and dry: these are eight, taken separately. And within it /fol. 7r./ there is the odd number seven, which is the odd number of the seven spheres: the sphere of Saturn, the sphere of Jupiter, the sphere of Mars, the sphere of the Sun, the sphere of Venus, the sphere of Mercury, and the sphere of the Moon; and it is the odd number of the seven days and of the seven earths and of everything sevenfold. And within it there is the odd number five, which is the odd number of the five prayers. And within it there is the odd number three, which is the odd number of the three abodes: the abode of this world, the abode of the barzakh, and the abode of the hereafter. And within it there is the odd number one, which is the intellect. Thus there are gathered in the sixteen seven evens and eight odds; and every even meets every odd, and every odd meets every even. An example of that: one and one are two, and three and three are six, and so on to the end of them; and likewise with the evens. And this is its numerical figure in the natural script, which is the Indian, in this form; and this script is the more fitting and the more proper for it.
[Figure.2 — the same 4×4 numerical square as above: 4, 14, 15, 1 / 9, 7, 6, 12 / 5, 11, 10, 8 / 16, 2, 3, 13]

And it has, in the letters, wondrous secrets — namely, that you set letters in the place of these numbers. Your working with them shall be after a fast of two weeks, in which by night you eat nothing but bread alone, together with the maintaining of ritual purity and the remembrance of God — exalted is He. Then you betake yourself to a square plate of refined tin and engrave upon it this literal figure, facing the qibla, after praying two rakʿas with the Throne Verse and Say: He is God, One (Q 112:1) a hundred times, on Thursday, in the hour of Jupiter, at sunrise, with the Moon safeguarded from Jupiter and from the Sun, and with the ascendant being Gemini; and you suffumigate it with mastic and white sandalwood every Thursday. Then the wearer of this ring — God, exalted is He, will make the affairs of religious observance beloved to him, and will make easy for him works and acts of obedience, and he will be granted ease

…in the means of livelihood, and God, exalted is He, will place blessing in whatever he undertakes with his hand. Likewise, if he sets it in his place of business, or in his shop, or in his strongbox, his wealth will grow great and his provision abundant — on condition that he write together with it the wording proper to the request for provision, for ample expansion, and for the placing of blessing, according to what comes hereafter, if God, exalted is He, wills.

Whoever writes it upon gazelle parchment on a Thursday at sunrise, and carries it with him sewn into his garments, will be kept safe, by the power of God, exalted is He, from thieves and from every hateful thing, and from all that he fears and is wary of — after he has written together with it the wording befitting it for all of that. And beware of carrying it in a state of ritual impurity. This is the first of the arrangements of the numbers. I shall inform you of something of the secrets of the numbers, and of what God, exalted is He, has brought forth within them, and of the description of their benefits and their operative deployments; and of the secret of the letters of the alphabet (al-ḥurūf al-muʿjama) that are in the Book of God, exalted is He — that is, the openings of the suras, which are twenty-eight suras — upon which none look save the elect among His creatures; and of what is contained in the Most Beautiful Names of God, exalted is He, which are the treasuries of the secrets /fol. 7v./ and the channels of the decrees; and of the knowledge of the Greatest Name of God, exalted is He, the Mighty, the Great, the Greater, the Generous, the Most Generous, and of what it contains of the divine secrets and the attributes of Lordship — such as you will not find in any book, nor light upon in any register, from what I have gathered and inscribed of the pearls of the sciences and the recondite secrets, so that whoever reads it and understands its meaning may profit by it.

This is the form of the letter-square (al-murabbaʿ al-ḥarfī), as you see. It has an invocation composed from its figure, assembled from its letters, which are these:(alif),(bāʾ),(jīm),(dāl),(hāʾ), (wāw), (zāy), (ḥāʾ),(ṭāʾ),(yāʾ) — the letter yāʾ having been added to them, it being the tenth.
[Wafq: 4×4, letter form — cells as in source; abjad values in parentheses] [Fig. 3]

And out of them the noble invocation is ordered. You say: "O God, I ask You by all Your Most Beautiful Names, those of them that I know and those that I do not know. Yā Hū, Yā Hū, Yā Wāḥid (O One), Yā Aḥad (O Unique), Yā Hādī (O Guide), Yā Barr (O Beneficent), Yā Bāriʾ (O Fashioner), Yā Baṣīr (O All-Seeing), Yā Badīʿ (O Wondrous Originator), Yā Bāsiṭ (O Expander), Yā Bāqī (O Abiding), Yā Jalīl (O Majestic), Yā Dāʾim (O Everlasting), Yā Wārith (O Inheritor), Yā Wadūd (O Loving), Yā Ḥayy (O Living), Yā Ḥalīm (O Forbearing), Yā Ḥaqq (O Truth), Yā
Ḥakīm (O Wise), Yā Ẓāhir (O Manifest), Yā Muẓhir (O Revealer). Fulfil my need! Answer, O Isrāfīl, you and your helpers and your servant-spirits from among the dwellers of the heavens and the earth!"

Now since it has already been set forth that the letters are twenty-eight, according to the number of the twenty-eight lunar mansions, that part of them which is visible above the earth is fourteen mansions, and beneath the earth fourteen mansions; so that when one mansion sets, the fifteenth, which is its counterpart, rises — thus for ever. For that reason fifteen of the letters are dotted and thirteen are undotted. The dotted ones are these:

. The undotted ones are these: .Those of them that are undotted are the mansions of the auspicious influences, and those of them that are dotted are the mansions of the inauspicious influences and of the mixed. Whichever of them has a single dot is nearer to the auspicious; whichever of them has two dots is intermediate among the inauspicious, and it is the mixed; and whichever of them has three dots is at the utmost — it is a greater malefic, as for example shīn ()and thāʾ (.)Ponder that. Here now I make plain to you the manner of it. It is this: that the mansions are figures of differing disposition within the divine creation, no one of them resembling another; whereas the moon — /fol. 8r./ God, exalted is He, created it round, and likewise the sun, for a hidden secret that cannot be expounded, because to divulge the secret of Lordship is unbelief. As for the moon, when it descends into the mansion of al-Naṭḥ, there are indications that point to it, and words [to be spoken]; but walls have ears, and concealment is the better course. So understand what we have indicated and ponder it. And God, exalted is He, speaks the truth, and He guides to the way.
Manbaʿ Uṣūl al-Ḥikma, vol. I, p. 15

The twenty-eight letters that exist are divided among the ʿanāṣir-i arbaʿa (the four elements), with seven (7) letters belonging to each element. These letters and the elements to which they belong are as follows:
[I 16] 1. The element of Fire: The letters belonging to this element are maftūḥ (open). They are dry and hot, of a choleric (ṣafrāwī) nature.
The direction of the fire letters is east; they are attracting and dominant.
The letters belonging to Fire are these:
Dhāl, Shin, Fe, Mīm, Ṭāʾ, He, Alif 2. The element of Earth: The letters belonging to this element are majzūm (cut off). They are dry and cold, of a melancholic (sawdāwī)
nature. The direction of the earth letters is south; they are attracted rather than attracting, and dominated.
The letters belonging to Earth are these:
Ḍād, Te, Sat, Nun, Ye, Wāw, Be 3. The element of Air: The letters belonging to this element are maghmūm (closed). They are moist and hot, of a sanguine (damawī)
nature. The direction of the air letters is west; they are attracting and dominant.
The letters belonging to Air are these:
Ẓāʾ, Se, Qāf, Sin, Kāf, Ze, Jīm 4. The element of Water: The letters belonging to this element are maksūr (broken). They are moist and cold, of a phlegmatic nature.
The direction of the water letters is north; they are attracted rather than attracting, and dominated.
The letters belonging to Water are these:
Ghayn, Khāʾ, Ra, ʿAyn, Lam, Ha, Dal
Manbaʿ Uṣūl al-Ḥikma, vol. I, p. 16
Of the twenty-eight (28) letters, fourteen (14) are set apart as nurani (luminous) and fourteen (14) as zulmani (dark).
Ye, He, Nun, Mīm, Lam, Kāf, Qāf, ʿAyn, Ṭāʾ, Sat, Sin, Ra, Ha, Alif The dark (zulmani) letters are these:
Wāw, Fe, ʿAyn, Ẓāʾ, Ḍād, Shin, Ze, Dhāl, Dal, Khāʾ, Jīm, Se, Te, Be
The Four Elements and Their Natures
Manbaʿ Uṣūl al-Ḥikma, vol. I, p. 17
The ʿAnāṣir Arbaʿa (Four Elements) are Fire, Earth, Air, and Water.
Each of these has its own nature.

The nature of Fire is dry and hot. The nature of Earth is dry and cold. The nature of Air is moist and hot. The nature of Water is moist and cold. Heat becomes mu'tedil (balanced, temperate) when joined with cold, and dryness when joined with moisture.

If the talib's element is fire and the maṭlūb's element is earth, the heat of the fire is tempered by the coldness of the earth. Two degrees of dryness remain, and the two cannot achieve harmony with one another.

If the talib's element is fire and the maṭlūb's element is air, the dryness of the fire is tempered by the moisture of the air. Two degrees of fire remain, and the two are in harmony with one another.

If the talib's element is fire and the maṭlūb's element is water, the heat of the fire is tempered by the coldness of the water; likewise the dryness of the fire is tempered by the moisture of the water, and the two are in harmony with one another.
If the talib's element is earth and the maṭlūb's element is fire, the coldness of the earth tempers the heat of the fire. Because two degrees of dryness remain, they can never achieve harmony.

If the talib's element is earth and the maṭlūb's element is air, the coldness of the earth is tempered by the heat of the air; likewise the dryness of the earth is tempered by the moisture of the air, and they achieve harmony.
If the talib's element is earth and the maṭlūb's element is water, the dryness of the earth is tempered by the moisture of the water.
Because two degrees of coldness remain, they can never achieve harmony.
If the talib's element is air and the maṭlūb's element is fire, the moisture of the air is tempered by the heat of the fire. Because two degrees of fire remain, they are in accord with one another.

[I 18] If the talib's element is air and the maṭlūb's element is earth, the heat of the air is tempered by the coldness of the earth; likewise the moisture of the air is tempered by the dryness of the earth, and they achieve harmony.
If the talib's element is air and the maṭlūb's is water, the heat of the air is tempered by the moisture of the water. Because two degrees of moisture remain, they are in accord with one another.

If the talib's element is water and the maṭlūb's element is fire, the coldness of the water tempers the heat of the fire; likewise the moisture of the water tempers the dryness of the fire, and they achieve harmony with one another.
If the talib's element is water and the maṭlūb's element is earth, the moisture of the water is tempered by the dryness of the earth.
Because two degrees of coldness remain, they cannot achieve harmony with one another.

If the talib's element is water and the maṭlūb's element is air, the coldness of the water is tempered by the heat of the air. Because two degrees of moisture remain, they achieve harmony with one another.

If the natures of the talib and the maṭlūb agree in heat or in moisture, they achieve harmony with one another. Fire with fire, earth with earth, air with air, water with water — these are always in harmony with one another.
The Friendship and Enmity of the Elements Toward One Another
Manbaʿ Uṣūl al-Ḥikma, vol. I, p. 18
Fire is a friend to Air and an enemy to Water. Earth is a friend to Water and an enemy to Air. Air is a friend to Fire and an enemy to Earth. Water is a friend to Earth and an enemy to Fire.
Chapter 2 (al-bāb al-thānī): On breaking and spreading (al-kasr wa- l-basṭ) and the ordering of the operations according to the [proper] times and hours

Know — may God grant me and you success in obedience to Him, in the understanding of His secrets, and in His providential care — that of the sun and the moon God, exalted is He, has spoken and has made mention of them in His Mighty Book, in His saying, exalted is He: "and the sun and the moon, each swimming in an orbit" (Q 21:33). This is because the moon, when it alights in the mansion of al-Naṭḥ— which is the letter (alif) — is [then] governed by the secret of the alif. So when it descends into that mansion, the spiritual force (rūḥāniyya) of the alif is disclosed from that mansion, and wrath appears throughout the parts of the world, and most of all among the noble and the great ones of the people of this world. Every one of created beings finds subjugation and contraction within his inward being, according to the mode proper to his human rank; and whoever examines this closely will find it so. A man ought therefore to keep still in that hour, to employ his bodily members in the worship of God, exalted is He, and in abundant remembrance of Him, and to keep to ritual purity in that hour. In it souls are contracted, so that a man does not know the cause of his contraction and becomes astonished within himself. That is because the alif is the first of the ranks of the units among the numbers and among the letters, so that it has no like; and for that reason it is through it that disquiet befalls the lower world. Understand that. In it, too, is the embittering (tanghīṣ) of whomever you wish to embitter among the people of this world and its most eminent, of the sort given to tyranny and arrogance; for it is suited to embittering him and to [drawing] profit from him — this because of the heat and dryness in the letter alif, on account of which the disquiet occurs and souls are contracted when the moon alights in it, and because of the heat and dryness in al-Naṭḥ; for it is the decan (wajh) of the Red One (al-Aḥmar, Mars), and the Red One is hot and dry, of the nature of fire, burning by its own kind.

So, if you invoke in it with hot, dry names of its own nature — when al-Naṭḥis rising upon the eastern horizon and the moon is in it — and you write the letter 111 times upon red copper, or upon iron, or upon a potsherd of red earthenware, in the name of the one you wish to embitter, and you place it in the fire after you have suffumigated it with something of its own kind, in which there is heat, such as khazaf (earthenware) and qaḍāb and the like; and you invoke with the names 111 times — these being the numbers that fall to the spreading (basṭ) of the alif. As for the names with which you invoke against him: it is that you take the letters of the name of the person mentioned, whom you wish to embitter and constrict, and spread them out, and look to see which of the natures predominates in his name — heat, or dryness, or cold, or moisture. Then you take /fol. 8v./ those hot and dry letters from his name and set them before you upon a tablet, and you add to them the letters of Mars (al-Mirrīkh), of al-Naṭḥ, and of the moon (al-qamar), and out of them you compose one of the names of God, exalted is He, and you invoke with it the number of times stated, and you gather your entire resolve (himma) upon crushing and subduing him.
An example of this: Zayd and ʿAmr. You set down the letters, separated and spread out, thus:

. These are fourteen letters. Of them, fiery are; earthy are ;of the hot-and-moist letters there are three, namely; and of the cold-and-moist letters there is one, namely.The hot letters, counted with their repetitions, were four:. The dry, with their repetitions, were six letters:

.The hot-and-moist are three, which are those written above; and the cold-and-moist is likewise as written, without repetition. So reckon up the fourteen letters: what predominates in these letters is heat and dryness. There came out for us, then, from the names of God, exalted is He, these. You say: I adjure you, O Samsamāʾīl, the [angelic] king, by Him who created you and fashioned you aright, and made you a light within your sphere, and singled you out with His might and bestowed it upon you — [I adjure you] that you be my helper in what I desire of you. For I have set you in power over So-and-so son of So-and-so, that you take vengeance upon him, and demolish his senses, and mingle with the heat of Mars in the heat of his nature, and stir up in him a fiery heat with which you crush his joints, and constrict with it his heart and his inward being, and destroy his mind; and that you bring down upon him the angels of chastisement and the fire of Mars, and set in motion against him fires and headache and all the other pains — by the right of Mars and the malefic influence and fire that is in it, and by the right of your mansion, lofty in measure, of dry heat, that takes vengeance upon the tyrannical oppressors and the transgressing despots. And send the spiritual beings of Mars, the masters of fire and chastisement and subjugation and affliction, against the spirit of this despot, transgressor, arrogant and tyrant; and let them give the chastisement of vengeance power over his body, and set over his inward being the secret of subjugation and wrath and vengeance. Truly I have adjured you by al-Qawī (the Strong), al-Muḥīṭ (the All-Encompassing), al-Ṭābiq (the Conforming), al-Ḥayy (the Living), al-Qayyūm (the Self-Subsisting), al-Nūr (the Light), al-Muʾmin (the Granter of Security), al-Muqaddim (the Promoter), al-Muʾakhkhir (the Deferrer), the Outpourer of lights and the Giver of secrets; and by the right of the fire and the sparks and the Red Planet; and by God, al-Wāḥid (the One), al-Qahhār (the All-Subduing): answer, O angels, obedient and swift, to the names of the Lord of the Worlds!
And you write together with it the five-by-five square (al-mukhammas).

Know, my brother — may God grant me and you success in obedience to Him — that the letter alif has an airy wafq; to it belongs the planet Mars, and its servant-spirit is al-Aḥmar (the Red One). It is a letter of powerful effect: when you multiply it by its like, it manifests obedience; and it is the limit of the units. Know, too, that this noble letter has power in the operative deployment (taṣrīf) of all the remaining letters, for it is like the father. Understand this. As for its occult properties: if you want it for love, you write it in this form, as we have set it out for you, in a /fol. 9r./ fortunate hour; and if you blend the name of the person for whom you are performing the operation together with the letter of the square, it is more beautiful and stronger in its effects. You say: I adjure you, O Samsamāʾīl, and your servant-spirits and your helpers of the celestial and of the terrestrial order, and all the servant-spirits of the letter alif; I adjure you that you hear and obey and stir up and disquiet — 252 — by the right of that by which I have adjured you, and by the right of the letter alif and the secrets that God, exalted is He, has sent down within it, upon which none looks save the lofty ones who know God; and by the right of abjad and the occult properties it contains: [I adjure you] that you answer with obedience to that to which I have summoned you, and by that with which I have adjured you. And judge by analogy with this whatever operations and acts are suited to it, and you will succeed, if God, exalted is He, wills, and your operation will succeed.

This is the wafq of the letter alif, whose secret and excellence are renowned among the learned. And if you want it for operations of corruption, do as we have mentioned and you will attain your object. God speaks the truth, and He guides to the way.

The second of the mansions is the mansion of al-Buṭayn, and to it belongs the letter (bāʾ). When the moon alights in it, there descends from it, by the leave of God, exalted is He, a spiritual power fit for wrath and for what has been mentioned above. In it medicine is drunk, and in it the great ones, the sons of this world, and the kings of the earth are stirred into motion, because this decan of Aries is the second, and it is the decan of the sun; in it falls the sun's exaltation, at six of its degrees, on the fourth day of April. The sun is benefic, save that it is hot and dry, of the nature of Mars. Because of its benefic quality and its exaltation in this decan, one works in it for acceptance and for gaining access to kings, for whatever you want of them and whatever you seek from them in it — for your needs will be granted. One works in it, too, for acts of love, for acceptance, and for the attraction of hearts; and strive by means of it toward whatever calls for that. It is also suitable for performing the philosophical arts (al-ṣināʿāt al-ḥikmiyya) and the golden elixirs and their regimen (tadbīr). /fol. 9v./

The third of the mansions is the mansion of al-Thurayyā, and to it belongs the letter (jīm). When the moon alights in it, there descends from it, by the command of God, exalted is He, a spiritual power compounded of heat and moisture, and a middling benefic influence, good for travel, for mingling with the nobles and gaining access to them, and to the great ones, the masters of this world, and the people of knowledge; for al-Thurayyā is an assembly of many stars, and therefore assembly with those we have mentioned is good in it. It has a mighty wafq, which is made during its exaltation and is carried, and with it one goes in upon the nobles; whoever carries it attains his object from them, and they love him and obey him in his affair, and none opposes him in what he wants and seeks. By it Abū Jaʿfar al-Barmakī was favoured with al-Rashīd, and obtained from him everything he wanted. This is the form of its layout, as you see. Understand, and you will be rightly guided, if God, exalted is He, wills.
